To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a deterioration in the information quality available to market participants can increase the likelihood of regime changes and, hence, reduce the stability of the economy.
the probability of a regime change is increasing in the noise in the information, and that the welfare implications of a regime change depend on the payoff structure.

(i) when crises potentially originate from a coordination failure and (ii) when a reduction in the information quality increases the likelihood of coordination failure, (iii) then a reduction in the level of information quality increases the risk of regime change and thus reduces stability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of information in the stability and welfare of financial markets.
how information quality and crises interact, and the results are relevant to a variety of contexts.
how the quality of information available to agents affects the stability of a system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the quality of information is important in the sense that the more accurate the information, the more likely the status quo is to survive, but the less important the information, the less likely the status quo will survive.
the effect of a deterioration in the information quality on the likelihood of a crisis is ambiguous and depends on the specific features of the economy.

information quality and crises in a game of regime change are related in a non-trivial way, and the direction of the relationship depends on the payoff structure of the game and on the quality of the fundamentals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
information quality is an important determinant of the stability of the economy.

the deterioration of information quality in a regime-change game can contribute towards the instability of the status quo, and that this is especially the case when the net payoff of the successful regime-change attack is more sensitive (less so) to the fundamentals than that of the status quo survival.
information quality is a crucial determinant of the stability of the economy and that a reduction in information quality is a potential source of economic instability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in a crisis, a deterioration in information quality is not necessarily a bad thing.

a deterioration in the information quality available to market participants can contribute towards instability in regime-change games, and this effect is more pronounced when there is a higher degree of uncertainty in the fundamentals.
, when crises originate from coordination failures and when there is a unique equilibrium, a deterioration in information quality may increase the likelihood of a crisis.
